entries.ipa: /əˈbʌv/ — the first syllable is always the reduced /ə/; no further weak form
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the fixed not above doing X idiom (she's not above lying). Never a finite clause. Also an adverb, adjective, and noun; the preposition alone takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] above [noun phrase] · [noun] above [noun phrase] · not above [verb-ing] · above all
entries.contrast: The above/over line is height versus alignment. Above asserts only that one thing is higher; over adds vertical alignment and often covering or crossing. For measurements and scales above is the word (above sea level, above average), while over takes quantities and counts (over fifty people). Against on: on requires contact, above forbids it.
entries.meaning: Higher than something, with air in between. That single geometric fact generates every other sense: higher on a map, higher on a measuring scale, higher in a hierarchy, and — by a short moral leap — too high in character to stoop to something. The one thing above never means is touching. Senses: 1. Higher than, without contact. 2. Higher on a scale of measurement. 3. Greater than a stated number or level. 4. Higher in rank, authority, or importance. 5. Too honorable or proud to do something. 6. Earlier on the page, in written reference.
examples: A hawk circled above the parking lot.
She keeps the good glasses above the microwave.
Denver is a mile above sea level.
The reservoir is twelve feet above normal.
Temperatures stayed above forty all week.
Anything above two hundred dollars needs a second signature.
A lieutenant is one grade above a sergeant.
She put the team above her own record.
He is not above taking credit for someone else's work.
No one in that office is above suspicion.
The exceptions noted above apply only to renewals.
Everything above this line is a draft.

entries.ipa: /əˈtɑp/, also /əˈtɔp/ — the first syllable is already /ə/; no further weak form
entries.register: formal or literary; common in journalism, rare in speech
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only. No gerund, no clause. Atop of is nonstandard.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] atop [noun phrase] · [noun] atop [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] atop [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Atop is on top of compressed into one word, and it is the more formal of the two. Unlike above it requires contact; unlike plain on it insists the surface is a high or prominent one.
entries.meaning: Resting on the highest surface of something, in contact with it. It is a written word — headlines, captions, nature writing, and real-estate copy love it — and it survives mainly because it is shorter than on top of and grander than on. It also has a small figurative life in the language of rankings and standings. Senses: 1. On the highest surface of a physical thing. 2. At the top of a ranking or standing (journalistic).
examples: A single crow sat atop the utility pole.
The chapel atop the hill is visible from the highway.
Snow lay six inches deep atop the woodpile.
She placed the last shingle atop the stack.
The company ended the quarter atop the industry.
He has stayed atop the rankings for three seasons.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈloʊ/, weak /bəˈloʊ/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. Also an adverb (the deck below, see below); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] below [noun phrase] · [noun] below [noun phrase] · below [number or level]
entries.contrast: The below/under line mirrors above/over. Below claims only lower position; under adds vertical alignment and often covering or containment. Measurements and scales take below (below freezing, below zero), while under takes quantities and ages (under thirty, under twenty dollars).
entries.meaning: Lower than something, with no claim about contact or alignment. Like its opposite above, it works on maps and on scales as readily as in the air: downstream is below, downhill is below, and any number smaller than the reference point is below it. It is the everyday word for lower position when nothing is doing any covering. Senses: 1. Lower than, without contact. 2. Farther down a slope, a river, or a coast. 3. Less than a stated number, level, or standard. 4. Lower in rank or grade. 5. Later on the page, in written reference.
examples: There is a crawlspace below the kitchen floor.
The clouds sat below the summit all morning.
The town lies just below the reservoir.
Fishing is better below the bridge than above it.
It stayed below freezing for nine days straight.
Her cholesterol is finally below two hundred.
No one below director level saw the memo.
He was two years below me in school.
See the table below for the current rates.
Everything below the dotted line is optional.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈniθ/, weak /bəˈniθ/ — the th is voiceless /θ/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No finite clause. A gerund appears only in the frozen disdain idiom (beneath answering) and is rare. Also an adverb.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] beneath [noun phrase] · [verb] beneath [noun phrase] · beneath [abstract noun]
entries.contrast: Beneath is the literary member of the under/underneath/below family and is almost never the natural spoken choice. What beneath owns outright is the moral sense (beneath contempt, beneath him), where under and below cannot go. It also handles the metaphor of a hidden interior better than either.
variants: 'neath /niθ/ — a poetic clipping that belongs to verse, hymn, and song lyric ('neath the willow); never write it in prose
entries.meaning: Directly under something, usually with the weight or nearness of the upper thing felt. It is under in a raised register, plus two senses of its own: the surface that conceals something, and the standard that something falls short of. Reach for it when you want the sentence to sound written rather than spoken. Senses: 1. Directly under, often with weight or pressure. 2. Under the surface of, hidden by an appearance. 3. Unworthy of, too low for someone's dignity.
examples: The ice groaned beneath their boots.
Roots had buckled the sidewalk beneath the maple.
Beneath the fresh paint, the wood was rotten.
Beneath all the legal language, the offer is simple.
That kind of gossip is beneath contempt.
He seemed to think manual labor was beneath him.

entries.ipa: /ˈoʊvər/ — no weak form; the r-colored /ɚ/ survives even unstressed, and the r-less /ˈoʊvə/ is British rather than an American reduction
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund (an argument over paying the bill, no control over spending) and a wh-clause (an argument over who pays, a fight over what to charge) in the dispute and authority senses. Never a that-clause — an argument over that he should pay is impossible; to hang a finite clause on it you need a noun to carry it (an argument over the claim that he should pay). Also an adverb (come over), an adjective (it's over), and a verb particle (think it over), none of which takes an object; the preposition always has one.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] over [noun phrase] · [noun] over [noun phrase] · over [number] · [choose/prefer] [X] over [Y] · stranded: the beam it hangs over
entries.contrast: Against above: over implies vertical alignment and permits covering, above asserts only greater height. Against on: on is contact and support, over is coverage from the top. Against under, its exact opposite in every sense here. On sense 9, against beyond: over the ridge names a barrier you would cross to get there, beyond the ridge names only what lies farther out and crosses nothing. Over is the most widely distributed word in this catalog: the path sense is in movement and direction, the span-of-time sense in time, the about sense in topic and reference, the bare quantity sense in agent, instrument, and manner, and the preference sense in comparison and opposition.
entries.meaning: Positioned higher than something and, characteristically, lined up with it — which is why over slides so easily into the idea of covering. From physical coverage it reaches authority (one person positioned over another), quantity (a number higher than another), preference (one option placed above another), the channel a message travels along, and the far side of any barrier you would have to go over to reach. The positional senses are collected here; the moving, temporal, topical, quantitative, and preferential senses are developed elsewhere in this catalog. Senses: 1. Higher than and vertically aligned with; spanning. 2. Covering, resting on top of and concealing. 3. Across the whole surface or extent of. 4. More than, with a number or amount (see also agent, instrument, and manner). 5. In a position of authority above. 6. Chosen or ranked ahead of an alternative (see also comparison and opposition). 7. By way of a channel or a medium. 8. Past and no longer troubled by. 9. On the far side of a barrier you would have to cross.
examples: The old sign still hangs over the entrance.
Power lines run over the whole subdivision.
He pulled the blanket over his head.
There was a tarp over the boat all winter.
A rash had spread over both arms by Tuesday.
Papers were scattered over every surface in the room.
The repair came to a little over nine hundred dollars.
Over half the class failed the first quiz.
No one over her signed off on the change.
He was given authority over both warehouses.
I'd take a long drive over a short flight any day.
The committee chose the local firm over two national ones.
They worked out the terms over the phone in ten minutes.
The alert went out over the emergency channel at four.
She is finally over the worst of the flu.
He is not over the layoff and may not be for a while.
Her cousins live over the border in Nogales.
The next town over the ridge has one gas station.

entries.ipa: /ˈʌndər/ — no weak form; casual speech drops the /d/ after the nasal, giving /ˈʌnɚ/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No finite clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (the boat went under) and a prefix (underpaid); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] under [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] under [noun phrase] · under [number or age] · under [authority] · under [process noun]
entries.contrast: Against below: under aligns and often covers, below only ranks lower. Against underneath: underneath is the emphatic physical form and has none of under's abstract senses. Against beneath: the same relation in a literary register. Scales take below (below freezing) while counts and ages take under (under thirty). Under has two other homes: the path sense (rolled under the fence) is in movement and direction, and the bare quantity sense (under fifty) reappears in agent, instrument, and manner.
entries.meaning: Directly lower than something and usually covered by it. That covering is what lets under become the workhorse abstraction of the group: things covered by an authority, by a rule, by a process, or by a heading are all under it. Of the four low-position words, this is by a wide margin the most useful and the most polysemous. Senses: 1. Directly below and typically covered by. 2. Worn or placed beneath another layer. 3. Less than a number, an age, or an amount. 4. Subject to the authority, rule, or command of. 5. Undergoing a stated process or condition. 6. Classified within a heading or a name.
examples: Your keys are under the newspaper.
We waited out the storm under an overpass.
She wore thermals under her jeans.
Put a towel under the pot before you set it down.
Anyone under eighteen needs a signed waiver.
We finished the job under budget for once.
The clinic operates under state supervision.
He served under three different chiefs.
The proposal is still under review.
Two of the three claims are under investigation.
You'll find it filed under "permits."
She published under a pen name for a decade.

entries.ipa: /ˌʌndərˈniθ/, also /ˈʌndərˌniθ/ before a noun; no vowel-reducing weak form, but casual speech drops the /d/ as in under, giving /ˌʌnɚˈniθ/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (look underneath) and a noun (the underneath of the car); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] underneath [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] underneath [noun phrase] · stranded: the mat it was underneath
entries.contrast: Underneath is the emphatic, strictly physical form of under: it insists that the upper thing covers and usually hides the lower one. It refuses every abstract sense under has — underneath new management, underneath thirty, and underneath investigation are all wrong. Against beneath, which says the same thing in a literary register, and below, which requires no covering at all.
entries.meaning: Directly under and covered by, with the covering emphasized. When someone says look underneath rather than look under, they mean the thing is hidden. The only figurative extension it allows is the one that keeps the covering metaphor intact: an outward appearance with something concealed behind it. Senses: 1. Directly under and concealed or covered by. 2. Behind an outward appearance.
examples: There is a whole box of photographs underneath the stairs.
She found the receipt underneath a stack of mail.
Something was rusting underneath the truck.
Underneath the gruffness he is a soft touch.
Underneath the confident delivery, the argument was thin.

entries.ipa: /əˈpɑn/, also /əˈpɔn/, weak /əˈpən/
entries.register: formal, literary, or legal; also fixed idioms at every register
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the immediately after sense (upon arriving, upon signing the lease). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] upon [noun phrase] · [verb] upon [noun phrase] · upon [verb-ing] · [noun] upon [same noun]
entries.contrast: Anywhere upon appears, on is also grammatical. Upon adds no meaning at all, only formality, so choose it for register, for rhythm, or because a fixed phrase demands it (once upon a time, row upon row). Against atop, which insists the surface is high; upon makes no such claim.
entries.meaning: A formal equivalent of on, identical in meaning and higher in register. It earns its keep in three places: legal and ceremonial prose, a set of fixed phrases that will not take on, and the "immediately after" construction with a gerund, where it is genuinely more idiomatic than on. Senses: 1. On a surface, in formal or literary style. 2. Immediately after (with a noun or gerund). 3. In fixed phrases and repeated-noun intensifiers.
examples: A heavy silence settled upon the room.
He laid the wreath upon the marker.
Upon signing, you receive the keys.
Upon further review, the call was reversed.
Wave upon wave of new applications came in.
Once upon a time there was a mill here.

entries.ipa: /əˈɡɛnst/, also /əˈɡeɪnst/, weak /əˈɡɛn(t)s/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (advised against going). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / lean / prop / rest] against [noun phrase] · [noun] against [noun phrase] · against [verb-ing] · stranded: the wall it was leaning against
entries.contrast: Against is the contact-under-pressure preposition. On is contact with support from below; against is contact with force from the side. Next to and beside are adjacency with no contact at all. For the backdrop sense nothing else will do. The forcible-motion sense is in movement and direction, and sense 3, opposition proper, is developed at length in comparison and opposition.
entries.meaning: Touching something and pressing on it. Everything in this entry is the resting state that force leaves behind: a thing leaning, a thing braced, a thing outlined by whatever sits behind it. From physical pressure the word generalizes to opposition of every kind, which is why the same syllable covers a ladder on a wall and a vote in a legislature. Senses: 1. Touching under pressure; leaning or braced. 2. Seen with something behind it as a backdrop. 3. In opposition to a rule, a person, or a side. 4. Providing protection or coverage from.
examples: Two shovels leaned against the garage door.
He stood with his back against the counter.
The pressed flowers show up beautifully against the dark paper.
Her red coat was the only color against all that snow.
Parking here is against the building rules.
Three of the five directors voted against the merger.
The policy protects against theft but not against flooding.
Everyone in the unit is vaccinated against hepatitis.

entries.ipa: /əˌlɔŋˈsaɪd/, also /əˌlɑŋˈsaɪd/; stress shifts to the first syllable before a noun
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the "at the same time as" sense (studied alongside working nights). No finite clause of any kind, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (a tug pulled alongside), which takes no object at all; the preposition always has one.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / pull / run] alongside [noun phrase] · [verb] alongside [noun phrase] · alongside [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Alongside adds parallel orientation to the plain adjacency of beside and next to: it wants two long things lying the same way. A chair beside the desk is fine; a chair alongside the desk implies the chair is lined up with it. Alongside of is redundant — drop the of. It is always one word.
entries.meaning: Beside and parallel to, close enough to be lined up with. Its nautical origin still governs the physical sense — you pull alongside a dock the way a hull comes to rest against a pier. The figurative senses keep the parallelism intact: people who work alongside each other are doing the same kind of thing at the same time, as equals rather than as one under the other, and once the equality drops away what is left is bare simultaneity — a document released alongside another one. Senses: 1. Beside and parallel to, physically. 2. Working or existing in parallel with, as an equal. 3. Together with; at the same time as.
examples: The tugboat eased alongside the freighter.
There is a drainage ditch alongside the whole east fence.
A photographer jogged alongside the lead runner.
He learned the trade alongside his father.
The new system will run alongside the old one until June.
She finished the degree alongside working two jobs.
The findings were published alongside a lengthy rebuttal.
The tax cut passed alongside a two-year spending freeze.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈsaɪd/, weak /bəˈsaɪd/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — beside me, never beside I. No clause, no gerund. Unlike besides, it is never an adverb.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / stand / walk] beside [noun phrase] · [noun] beside [noun phrase] · beside the point · beside [reflexive]
entries.contrast: Beside and besides are different words, and confusing them is the most common error in this category. Beside is position — at the side of. Besides is addition or exception. If next to fits, the word is beside; if in addition to fits, the word is besides.
entries.meaning: At the side of something, close by. It is the plainest adjacency word in English and carries no implication of contact, alignment, or facing. Two idioms have drifted away from the literal sense and are worth learning whole: beside the point, meaning irrelevant, and beside oneself, meaning overcome by an emotion. Senses: 1. At the side of; next to. 2. Compared with (a slightly formal use). 3. In the fixed idioms beside the point and beside oneself.
examples: There is a bench beside the trailhead.
Park beside the blue truck and walk up.
The first draft looks amateurish beside the final version.
A two-hour delay is nothing beside what they went through.
Whether he meant it is beside the point.
She was beside herself when the dog came back.

entries.ipa: /ˈfeɪsɪŋ/ — no weak form; like every participial preposition it keeps the shape of its verb
entries.register: neutral; the standard word in real-estate, architectural, seating, and travel description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — facing the park, facing us. No clause, no gerund. One warning is worth the whole entry: the company is facing a recall is the verb face in the progressive, not this preposition. The test is substitution — if opposite or across from can replace it without touching the rest of the clause, it is the preposition (a cabin facing the lake, a cabin across from the lake); if only confronting fits, it is the verb.
entries.pattern: [noun] facing [noun phrase] · [be-verb] facing [noun phrase] · [sit / stand / park] facing [noun phrase] · [page / plate] facing [page number]
entries.contrast: Facing is the participial member of the opposite / across from group, and the one that states orientation outright. Opposite and across from only put two things on either side of a gap; facing says which way the thing is turned. A house can be across from the park and still show it a blank wall, but a house facing the park looks at it. Against before, the formal and largely ceremonial word for the same geometry. Against the near-twin overlooking, which adds height and a downward view — a room overlooking the harbor is above it, a room facing the harbor need not be. Against toward, which is orientation with motion implied; facing is orientation at rest. Note the spelling there: toward is the American form and towards the British one, and the same split runs through amid/amidst, among/amongst, and around/round in this file.
entries.meaning: Turned toward something and looking at it across an intervening space. The word has quietly taken over the work American English has been withdrawing from opposite, and it does that work with the orientation made explicit, which is why floor plans, seating charts, and listings reach for it so often. It stays close to its verb: whatever does the facing is understood to have a front. Senses: 1. Turned toward; looking out at. 2. On the side of a structure that looks toward something. 3. Directly opposite in a printed or laid-out spread.
examples: They asked for a room facing the courtyard.
He sat facing the door for the whole meal.
Two lots facing the water sold in the first week.
All the offices facing the parking lot get afternoon glare.
The bleachers facing the visitors' bench were empty by the fifth.
The map on the page facing the index is out of date.
The photograph facing the title page was taken in 1911.

entries.ipa: /nɪr/ — no weak form; the vowel stays full even unstressed
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; also a fused relative — a wh-clause standing in for a noun phrase — in the degree use: nowhere near what we needed, not anywhere near what it cost. Never a that-clause, and a gerund is marginal at best: came near winning is idiomatic, but near finishing the report is not. Alone among the simple prepositions, near is gradable and inflects for degree — nearer the door, nearest the exit. It is also an adjective, an adverb, and a verb.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] near [noun phrase] · [noun] near [noun phrase] · nearer / nearest [noun phrase] · near to [noun phrase] · nowhere near [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Near and close to are interchangeable in most sentences; near is shorter and takes the comparative directly (nearer the fire). Against by, which means immediately beside. Against beside, which is adjacency with no distance at all. Nearby is not a preposition in careful American English.
variants: near to (chiefly British and slightly formal in American English; bare near is the American default)
entries.meaning: Not far from, in space, in time, or on a scale of condition. It is the vaguest of the proximity words and that vagueness is the point: near the airport commits to nothing about how near. Its gradability is what sets it apart from every other preposition in this file, and it is the reason near survives in a class that otherwise refuses comparison. Senses: 1. Not far from in space. 2. Not far from in time. 3. Close to a state, a condition, or a number.
examples: There's a decent diner near the courthouse.
Sit nearer the front if you want to hear.
The fire started somewhere near the fuse box.
It was near midnight before anyone left.
Near the end of the season he tore a hamstring.
She was near tears by the time she finished.
The bid came nowhere near what we needed.

entries.ipa: /ˌnɪrˈbaɪ/ as an adverb, /ˈnɪrˌbaɪ/ as an attributive adjective
entries.register: neutral as adjective and adverb; the prepositional use is nonstandard in American English
entries.complement: As a preposition it takes a noun phrase — but do not use it that way. Nearby the station is regularly flagged as an error by American editors; write near the station. In its standard lives it takes no object at all: adjective before a noun, adverb after the verb.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] is nearby (adverb) · a nearby [noun] (adjective) · avoid: nearby [noun phrase] (preposition)
entries.contrast: The rule is short: near takes an object, nearby does not. A store near the school and a nearby store are both correct; a store nearby the school is the error. A preposition has an object, an adverb stands alone.
entries.meaning: Close at hand. It is listed here because learners reach for it as a preposition and American editors take it back out. Treat it as an adjective and an adverb, and hand the prepositional work to near. Its inclusion in a preposition dictionary is a warning label, not an endorsement. Senses: 1. Adverb: at a short distance, with no object. 2. Adjective before a noun: located close at hand. 3. Preposition (nonstandard in American English): near.
examples: We ate at a taqueria nearby.
Is there a gas station nearby?
A nearby fire station handled the call.
Two nearby counties reported the same outage.
Nonstandard: they camped nearby the lake. Standard: they camped near the lake.
Nonstandard: the office is nearby the courthouse. Standard: the office is near the courthouse.

entries.ipa: /ˈɑpəzɪt/, also /ˈɑpəsɪt/ — the final syllable is reduced in every American pronunciation
entries.register: neutral, but the spatial preposition sounds British or formal in American English
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adjective, a noun, and an adverb.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] opposite [noun phrase] · [noun] opposite [noun phrase] · [act / play / star] opposite [person] · opposite to / from [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: For the spatial sense, American English says across from, or facing when the orientation matters. The bank across from the courthouse is the ordinary American sentence; the bank opposite the courthouse reads as British or formal. What is fully American is the casting sense — she played opposite Denzel Washington.
variants: opposite to, opposite from (both acceptable; bare opposite is the standard prepositional form)
entries.meaning: Facing something from the other side of a space between. The space matters: things opposite each other are separated and turned toward one another, which is why the word works for seats at a table, buildings on a street, and actors sharing a scene. Americans keep the second of those senses and quietly hand the first to across from. Senses: 1. Facing, on the other side of a space (chiefly British in this use). 2. As the counterpart of another performer.
examples: She took the chair opposite mine.
The hotel stands opposite the train station.
There is a small park opposite the school gates.
She was cast opposite an actor she had never met.
Playing opposite him was the best part of the job.

entries.ipa: /ˌoʊvɚˈlʊkɪŋ/ — no weak form; the vowel of look is the lax /ʊ/ of book
entries.register: neutral; the standard word in real-estate, hotel, and travel description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — overlooking the bay, overlooking us. No clause of any kind, and no gerund: the thing seen is always a noun phrase (overlooking the harbor), never a verb. The same warning that governs facing governs this word: the auditor is overlooking a whole account is the verb overlook in the progressive, not this preposition. The test is substitution — if with a view of can replace it without touching the rest of the clause, it is the preposition (a terrace overlooking the river); if only failing to notice fits, it is the verb.
entries.pattern: [noun] overlooking [noun phrase] · [be-verb] overlooking [noun phrase] · [sit / stand / perch] overlooking [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Overlooking is facing plus height. Both say which way the thing is turned, but overlooking adds that it is above what it sees and looks down at it: a room facing the harbor may be at sea level, a room overlooking the harbor is not. Against above, which is height with no view and no orientation at all. Against over, which is height with alignment and no viewer. Against opposite and across from, which need a gap but neither elevation nor orientation. Keep the two lives of the word apart: as a preposition it gives you a view, as a verb it means you missed something.
entries.meaning: Above something and looking down at it. Its whole meaning is what facing and above deliver together, which is why American listings reach for it any time there is a view to sell. The object is always the thing seen and never the viewer, and whatever does the overlooking is understood to have both a front and a vantage point — which is how the word came to work for terrain and fortifications as easily as for windows. Senses: 1. Situated above and giving a view of. 2. Standing high above and dominating, with no viewer implied.
examples: They booked a room overlooking the courtyard.
Her office is on the ninth floor, overlooking the river.
We ate on a terrace overlooking the vineyard.
The old fort sits on a bluff overlooking the harbor entrance.
A water tower overlooking the interchange is the only landmark for miles.
Guns were dug in along the ridge overlooking the valley floor.

entries.ipa: /əˈbɔrd/ — the first syllable is always /ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (all aboard, welcome aboard).
entries.pattern: [be-verb] aboard [vessel or vehicle] · [verb of motion] aboard [vessel] · aboard (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: Aboard is the vehicle-specific member of the in/on system: you are in a car, on a bus or a plane, and aboard a ship, plane, train, or spacecraft. For the figurative sense of joining a team, American English overwhelmingly writes on board.
variants: on board (two words; identical in meaning, and the dominant form in the figurative business sense — bring her on board)
entries.meaning: On or inside a vessel or a large vehicle. It covers both the static position and the act of getting there, which is why the same word does everyone aboard survived and she came aboard in Seattle. The figurative use — joining an organization — is a live metaphor that most writers now spell as two words. Senses: 1. On or inside a ship, plane, train, or bus. 2. As a member of a crew, team, or organization (figurative).
examples: Everyone aboard the flight was accounted for.
The equipment stayed aboard the research vessel all winter.
She was the last passenger aboard the train.
Welcome aboard — your badge is at the front desk.
Two new engineers came aboard this month.

entries.ipa: /əˈmɪd/; amidst /əˈmɪdst/ — both keep the schwa in the first syllable
entries.register: formal or literary in the physical sense; standard journalism in the background-events sense
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically a mass noun or a plural (amid the wreckage, amid rising costs). No clause, no gerund.
entries.pattern: amid [mass noun] · amid [plural noun phrase] · amid [event noun]
entries.contrast: The amid/among split is countability. Amid surrounds you with something undifferentiated — wreckage, smoke, chaos; among surrounds you with individuals you could point at. Amid also sets a scene of ongoing events behind a piece of news (amid falling revenues), which among cannot.
variants: amidst — chiefly British and slightly more literary; American English prefers amid, and the two are otherwise identical
entries.meaning: In the middle of something that is treated as a mass rather than counted. The physical sense is literary and slightly old-fashioned in speech, but the abstract one is everywhere in news writing, where amid is the standard way to hang a story on a backdrop of continuing conditions without claiming a causal link. Senses: 1. Surrounded by, in the middle of a mass. 2. Against a background of continuing events or conditions.
examples: They found the ring amid the ashes.
A single lit window amid all that darkness.
Shares fell amid growing concern about the supply chain.
The mayor resigned amid questions about the contract.
Talks resumed amid signs that both sides were tiring.

entries.ipa: /əˈmʌŋ/; amongst /əˈmʌŋst/ — the first syllable is always /ə/ and never stressed
entries.complement: a plural, collective, or mass noun phrase — among the trees, among the staff, among us. Among the tree is ungrammatical: the object must denote more than one thing. Objective pronouns only. No clause, no gerund.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] among [plural noun phrase] · [divide / share / distribute] [object] among [plural noun phrase] · among [plural] · among other things
entries.contrast: The rule between for two, among for more is only half true. Between is correct for any number when the parties are individually in view and the relation is one-to-one (a treaty between six nations). Among is the word when the group is undifferentiated. Against amid: among counts its objects, amid does not.
variants: amongst — chiefly British; it is not wrong in American English but it is markedly bookish, and edited American prose uses among
entries.meaning: Surrounded by or included in a group of more than one. Its four senses all follow from that: physically in the middle of a group, a member of a set, a share distributed to a group, and a trait holding across a group. The one hard requirement is plurality — whatever follows among must be countable as more than one or collective in meaning. Senses: 1. In the middle of, surrounded by a group. 2. Included in a set; one of. 3. Distributed to the members of a group. 4. Holding across the members of a group.
examples: We found him among the crowd at the gate.
A few red maples stood out among all the oaks.
Her novel is among the best things published that year.
Among other duties, he handles scheduling.
Split the tips evenly among the servers.
The land was parceled out among six families.
Turnout was highest among voters over sixty.
Sleep problems are widespread among shift workers.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈtwin/, weak /bəˈtwin/; the literary clipping 'tween /twin/
entries.complement: a plural noun phrase (between the buildings), or two or more noun phrases joined by and — never by or. Objective pronouns only: between you and me, never between you and I. Gerunds are fine as coordinates (torn between working and commuting), and so are fused relatives: the difference between what he said and what he did. Never a that-clause. Also an adverb with no object at all (a fence with a gate in between, the years between), and the preposition always has one.
entries.pattern: between [X] and [Y] · between [plural noun phrase] · between [pronoun] and [pronoun] · in between [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Three errors cluster here. Between you and I is wrong — a preposition takes the objective case: between you and me. The coordinator must be and, not or. Ranges take and, not to: between 1990 and 1995, or from 1990 to 1995. On between vs. among, the deciding factor is whether the parties are individually in view, not how many there are.
entries.meaning: In the space, the interval, or the relationship separating two or more distinct things that are individually in view. That last clause is what really governs the word — between keeps its objects separate and named, which is why it works for gaps, for treaties, for choices, and for joint efforts, and why it is fine with six parties as long as you can point at each one. Senses: 1. In the physical space separating two or more things. 2. In the interval separating two times or points (see also time). 3. Connecting or dividing two or more parties, reciprocally. 4. Marking a choice among named alternatives. 5. Pooling the resources or efforts of a set of people.
examples: A narrow gap between the fence and the shed lets the water through.
She was sitting between her two brothers.
Call me between nine and eleven.
There were four collisions on that stretch between January and March.
The treaty between the six nations took a decade to draft.
Whatever is said between you and me stays here.
He had to choose between the job in Denver and the one in Austin.
There is not much to choose between the two proposals.
Between them they own half the block.
Between the deposit and the first month's rent, it came to three thousand.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈtwɪkst/, weak /bəˈtwɪkst/
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in modern American English only in the fixed phrase betwixt and between
entries.complement: the same as between — a plural noun phrase or two noun phrases joined by and, with objective pronouns. No clause, no gerund.
entries.pattern: betwixt [X] and [Y] · betwixt [plural noun phrase] · betwixt and between (fixed idiom)
entries.contrast: Betwixt is between in period costume. It means exactly the same thing and has no context in which it is the better choice for ordinary prose. The one exception is the reduplicated idiom betwixt and between, meaning undecided, which is still current.
entries.meaning: An archaic form of between, kept alive by poetry, by deliberate period flavor, and by one surviving idiom. Learners should be able to recognize it in older texts and should not produce it. Note that the idiom betwixt and between has drifted away from the preposition entirely and now works as an adjective phrase. Senses: 1. Archaic or literary: between. 2. In the fixed phrase betwixt and between: undecided, in an awkward middle state.
examples: The old deed describes the parcel as lying betwixt the river and the road.
There is little to choose betwixt the two, as an older writer would have put it.
Betwixt dawn and full light the whole field was white with frost.
She has quit one job and not started the next, so she is betwixt and between.
The design is betwixt and between — too plain for a gallery, too fussy for a kitchen.

entries.ipa: /ɪnˈsaɪd/ as preposition and adverb, /ˈɪnsaɪd/ as noun and attributive adjective
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (come inside), a noun, and an adjective; the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] inside [noun phrase] · [verb of motion] inside [noun phrase] · inside of [period of time] · stranded: the box it was inside
entries.contrast: Against in: in is the neutral container word, inside insists on the enclosure and implies a contrasting outside. Only in can go abstract — in trouble, in love have no inside version. Against within: inside is physical enclosure, within is limits and abstractions. Against into: inside is where something is, into is where it is going.
variants: inside of — informal in the spatial sense (drop the of in edited prose); idiomatic and standard in the time sense, inside of an hour
entries.meaning: Within the bounds of a container, a building, or a boundary, with the boundary itself in the picture. It is the emphatic counterpart of in and the exact opposite of outside, and it keeps that contrast in every sense — a physical interior, the interior of an organization, and, in one informal American use, the interior of a stretch of time. Senses: 1. Within the bounds of a container or enclosed space. 2. Within an organization, as opposed to outside it. 3. In less than a stated period of time (informal, usually inside of).
examples: Everything you need is inside the blue folder.
Wait inside the building until they call your name.
Sources inside the agency describe a very different timeline.
The decision was made inside the family, not by the board.
The whole repair was done inside of twenty minutes.
If we leave now we'll be there inside of two hours.

entries.ipa: /ˌaʊtˈsaɪd/ as preposition and adverb, /ˈaʊtˌsaɪd/ as noun and attributive adjective
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the "apart from" sense only, and there almost always with of — outside of being tired, I'm fine. No clause of any kind, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (wait outside), a noun, and an adjective; the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] outside [noun phrase] · [verb] outside [noun phrase] · outside of [noun phrase] · outside [abstract limit]
entries.contrast: The mirror image of inside. On outside vs. outside of: American speech uses both freely, but editors delete the of in he waited outside the courthouse. The apart-from sense (outside of a few complaints) is the one place the of is normal.
variants: outside of — extremely common in American speech; edited prose drops the of for the spatial and scope senses, but keeps it for the "apart from" sense, where besides or apart from is cleaner still
entries.meaning: Beyond the bounds of something — a building, a boundary, a jurisdiction, or a scope. The physical sense is the base; the scope sense (outside my expertise, outside the law) is where the word does most of its work in adult prose, because it draws a limit and puts something firmly past it. Senses: 1. Beyond the physical bounds of. 2. Beyond the scope, limits, or authority of. 3. Apart from, other than (usually outside of).
examples: There were reporters outside the building all afternoon.
The house sits just outside the city limits.
Anything over a hundred pounds is outside the elevator's rating.
Enforcement of that rule is outside our authority.
Outside of the opening chapter, the book holds up.
Outside of Tuesday, I'm free all week.

entries.ipa: /wɪˈðɪn/, weak /wəˈðɪn/ — the th is voiced /ð/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (inquire within).
entries.pattern: within [bounded area] · within [distance or measure] · within [period of time] · within [organization or person]
entries.contrast: The heart of this entry is in versus within. In three days means three days from now; within three days means at any point before three days have elapsed — a deadline, not a date. Spatially, in locates and within bounds: in the city says where you are, within the city limits says which side of a line you are on.
entries.meaning: Inside the limits of something. The limits are the point: within always implies a boundary you have not crossed, whether that boundary is a city line, a budget, a tolerance, a deadline, or the edge of an organization. It is the preposition of not-exceeding, and that is why contracts, specifications, and regulations lean on it so heavily. Senses: 1. Inside the bounds of an area. 2. Inside a range or a measured limit. 3. Before a stated period has elapsed (see also time). 4. Inside a person, a group, or an organization.
examples: Everything within the fence line belongs to the county.
The site is within a mile of the river.
The project finished within budget by about four percent.
Keep the reading within tolerance or the batch is rejected.
Payment is due within thirty days of invoice.
She had three offers within a week of posting her resume.
The split within the party is wider than it looks.
He kept the anger within himself for years.

entries.ipa: /wɪˈðaʊt/, weak /wəˈðaʊt/ — the th is voiced /ð/
entries.register: archaic or literary in this spatial sense; the modern "lacking" sense is fully neutral and lives in accompaniment and exception
entries.complement: in the spatial sense, a noun phrase only — without the walls, without the gates. No clause, no gerund in this sense. Also an adverb in the fixed pairing within and without.
entries.pattern: without [walls / gates / city] (archaic spatial) · within and without (fixed adverbial pair)
entries.contrast: This entry covers only the obsolete sense outside of, the exact opposite of within. In living American English that job belongs entirely to outside; without the city now reads as archaic. The productive modern sense (without money, without asking) is treated in accompaniment and exception.
entries.meaning: Outside of, beyond the bounds of. This was once the ordinary opposite of within, and the two words still show their shared architecture. It survives in scripture, in older legal descriptions of land, in hymn and poetry, and in the frozen pair within and without. Recognize it; do not write it. Senses: 1. Archaic: outside of, beyond the walls or bounds of. 2. In the fixed adverbial pair within and without: inside and outside alike.
examples: The old charter refers to the parishes without the walls.
They buried him without the churchyard, as the custom then required.
A green hill far away, without a city wall.
The ship was rebuilt within and without.
She was calm within and without, whatever it cost her.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈfɔr/, weak /bəˈfɔr/, and /bfɔr/ in fast speech
entries.register: formal, legal, ceremonial, or literary in the spatial sense; the temporal sense is neutral and lives in time
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. In the spatial sense there is no gerund. Never a finite clause after the preposition; before he arrived is the subordinating conjunction, a different word class with the same spelling.
entries.pattern: [stand / appear / kneel] before [noun phrase] · [noun] before [noun phrase] · [X] comes before [Y] (order)
entries.contrast: In modern American English the ordinary spatial word is in front of, not before. Spatial before survives in courtrooms and hearings, in ceremony and scripture, and in the metaphor of a task facing someone. Before is a preposition with a noun phrase, a conjunction with a clause, and an adverb with nothing.
entries.meaning: In front of, in the physical or figurative presence of. The spatial sense is the older one and has been largely displaced in speech by in front of, retreating into formal registers where its stiffness is an asset. Two live uses remain fully current: appearing before an authority, and a task or choice standing before a person. Senses: 1. In front of, in the presence of (formal). 2. Earlier in a sequence or order. 3. Facing someone as a task, choice, or prospect.
examples: The witness appeared before the grand jury on Thursday.
He knelt before the altar.
In the alphabet, M comes before N.
Safety comes before speed on this crew.
The choice before us is not a comfortable one.
A long winter lay before them.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈhaɪnd/, weak /bəˈhaɪnd/, and /bəˈaɪnd/ in very fast speech with the /h/ dropped
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the cause sense (the thinking behind closing the plant, the money behind building the arena). No finite clause — write behind the decision to close, never behind they decided to close, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (he stayed behind) and a noun; the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] behind [noun phrase] · [verb] behind [noun phrase] · behind [schedule / on rent] · behind [person] · stranded: the door he was hiding behind
entries.contrast: Against after: after orders things in time or sequence, behind places them in space or measures a lag. Against beyond and past, which put something on the far side of a thing rather than at its back. Note the American variant in back of, standard in speech and jarring to British ears.
variants: in back of — a genuinely American alternative for the spatial sense, common in speech and regionally strong; unknown in British English and avoided in formal writing
entries.meaning: At the back of something, on the side away from the front or from the observer. From that position the word picks up four extensions that all preserve the geometry: falling back in a race or a schedule, standing back of someone in support, working back of a public event as its hidden cause, and putting an experience back of you in the past. Senses: 1. At the back of, on the far side of. 2. Later or slower than; in arrears (see also time). 3. Supporting, backing. 4. Responsible for, as the hidden cause or agent. 5. In the past, left behind.
examples: There is a small yard behind the building.
She hid the box behind a stack of paint cans.
The Rangers finished nine games behind the leaders.
He fell behind on rent after the layoff.
The union is solidly behind the proposal.
Get behind this or get out of the way.
Investigators still do not know who was behind the transfer.
There is a real grievance behind all the shouting.
Those years are behind her and she does not discuss them.
Once the audit is behind us we can hire again.

entries.ipa: /biˈɑnd/, also /bɪˈjɑnd/ and /bɪˈjɔnd/, weak /bəˈjɑnd/
entries.respell: bee-AHND; also bih-YAHND, bih-YAWND; weak buh-YAHND
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (beyond saving), or a wh-clause (beyond what she told us). Never a that-clause. Also an adverb and a noun.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] beyond [noun phrase] · beyond [abstract limit] · beyond [verb-ing] · beyond [wh-clause] · go beyond [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against past: past is close and dynamic, beyond is static and farther out and dominates the abstract senses. Against outside: outside draws a boundary around a category, beyond draws a threshold something has exceeded. Beyond takes a wh-clause, which is why beyond what he admitted is fine while beyond that he admitted is not.
entries.meaning: On the far side of something, and by extension past any limit at all. It is one of the most abstractly productive prepositions in English: once the literal sense of "farther than" is in place, everything that can have a limit — repair, belief, control, expectation, dispute — can be beyond it. The frozen phrases (beyond repair, beyond belief, beyond doubt) are worth learning as units. Senses: 1. On the far side of; farther away than. 2. Later than a point in time. 3. Outside the limits, scope, or reach of. 4. More than; surpassing. 5. Apart from, other than (usually in a negative).
examples: There is nothing beyond the last cattle guard but sagebrush.
The trail continues a half mile beyond the falls.
Deliveries do not run beyond six o'clock.
He stayed beyond his welcome by about two hours.
The engine was beyond saving.
That decision is beyond my authority.
Her generosity went beyond anything the family asked for.
The results exceeded the forecast beyond all reason.
Beyond a short statement, the company has said nothing.
I remember nothing beyond what I already told the officer.

entries.ipa: /pæst/ — no weak form; the final /t/ drops before a consonant, giving /pæs/, which is why past and passed are confused
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund only in a short frozen list — past caring, past saving, past praying for — which is not a productive pattern. No clause of any kind. Also an adverb (he walked past), an adjective (the past year), and a noun (in the past) — only the preposition has an object, which is the test: he walked past is the adverb, he walked past the church is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] past [noun phrase] · [noun] past [landmark] · just past [noun phrase] · past [abstract limit] · put it past [someone]
entries.contrast: The spelling trap first: passed is the verb, past is everything else. We passed the church (verb) but we drove past the church (preposition). If you can put did in front of it, you want passed. Against beyond: past is near and reckoned from a landmark you have just cleared, beyond is farther out and more abstract.
entries.meaning: On the far side of a landmark, reckoned from it. The positional sense is essentially how Americans give directions — everything is past the light, past the bank, just past the second stop sign — and it depends on a shared reference point in a way beyond does not. The same geometry then runs along scales instead of streets (past forty, past its expiration date), and a short frozen list (past caring, past saving, wouldn't put it past her) preserves the oldest sense of having gone beyond a limit for good. Senses: 1. On the far side of a landmark; farther along than. 2. Beyond a point on a scale, an age, or a stage of life. 3. Beyond the point of, in the frozen gerund and idiom set.
examples: The mailbox is just past the church on the right.
Their driveway is a hundred yards past the cattle guard.
Go past the second stop sign and it's on your left.
That pitcher is past his prime and everyone knows it.
The milk is well past its date.
She was past fifty before she learned to swim.
He is past caring what the committee thinks.
The transmission was past saving by the time they looked at it.
I wouldn't put it past her to call the mayor herself.

entries.ipa: /əˈkrɔs/, also /əˈkrɑs/ — the first syllable is already /ə/; no further weak form; acrosst is nonstandard
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (he swam across). In the facing sense the object attaches to from: across from the school.
entries.pattern: [noun] across [noun phrase] (spanning) · across from [noun phrase] (facing) · across [area or group] (distribution) · [be-verb] across [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against through: across treats its object as a two-dimensional surface you cover the face of, through treats it as a three-dimensional medium you pass inside — across the field, through the woods. Against along: across cuts a line, along follows it. Contact is optional and the senses split on it: sense 1 usually has none (a bridge across the canyon), sense 4 always has it (arms folded across his chest). Across from is the everyday American way to say facing, where British English uses opposite.
variants: acrost, acrosst — dialectal and nonstandard; never write them
entries.meaning: Spanning something from one side to the other, or positioned on the far side of it. The static senses collected here are what is left when the motion drains out of the word: a bridge that has already crossed, a scar that already spans a cheek, a store that already sits on the other side of the street. The third sense — distribution over a whole area or population — is now heavy in business and news prose, and the fourth is the one case where across insists on contact. Senses: 1. Extending from one side to the other; spanning. 2. On the other side of; facing (usually across from). 3. Distributed over the whole of an area or group. 4. Lying transversely on something, in contact with it.
examples: There is a fallen pine across the driveway.
A long scar ran across the back of his hand.
They live across the street from us.
Her office is across the hall.
Costs rose across all six divisions.
The policy applies across the entire system.
He listened with his arms folded across his chest.
She had a wool blanket across her knees for the whole drive.

entries.ipa: /əˈlɔŋ/, also /əˈlɑŋ/ — the first syllable is always /ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — and the object must be something with length: a road, a river, a wall, a shelf. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb and verb particle (come along, bring it along), where it has no object at all.
entries.pattern: [noun] along [linear object] · [verb] along [linear object] · somewhere along [linear object] · all along [linear object]
entries.contrast: The object has to be long. Along the fence works; along the room does not — and the figurative objects obey the same rule, since a way, a line, a spectrum, and a continuum are all lines. Against across, which cuts the line rather than following it. Against alongside, which requires two separate parallel things. In bring it along, along has no object and is not a preposition.
entries.meaning: Following the length of something, or located at some point on that length. The senses are really one geometry seen at different scales — the whole line, a spot on it, or a line that exists only in the mind. What unites every use is that the object must be linear; the moment it is not, the sentence stops working. Senses: 1. In a line following the length of something. 2. At an unspecified point on the length of something. 3. At a point on a notional line, scale, or continuum (figurative).
examples: There are streetlights along the whole east side of the park.
Fenceposts run along the property line for a mile.
She lined the books up along the top shelf.
Somewhere along Route 6 we missed the turn.
The pipe froze at a joint along the north wall.
The trail loses elevation gradually all along the ridge.
The new proposal is along the same lines as last year's.
Somewhere along the way the project lost half its budget.

entries.ipa: /əˈraʊnd/; in casual speech the first syllable can drop entirely, giving /ˈraʊnd/ ('round)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; also a bare number or clock time in the approximation sense (around noon, around fifty), and a gerund in the jargon sense 5 (questions around hiring contractors). No clause, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (look around) and a particle; the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] around [noun phrase] · [noun] around [noun phrase] · around [number or time] · around here / there · around the corner
entries.contrast: Use around, not round, in American English for every physical sense. For approximation, around and about are both American and interchangeable, with around commoner in speech. A conversation around funding is business jargon that many editors delete in favor of about.
variants: round — chiefly British for the physical senses; see its own entry
entries.meaning: Encircling something, or scattered in its vicinity. From the circle come two useful extensions: getting to the far side by going around an obstruction, and — because a circle drawn around a number is a rough boundary rather than a point — approximation. It is one of the highest-frequency prepositions in American speech and one of the vaguest. Senses: 1. Encircling; on all sides of. 2. Scattered in the vicinity of; here and there in. 3. On the other side of, reached by going along a curve. 4. Approximately, with a number or a time (see also time). 5. Centered on a topic (business jargon; prefer about).
examples: They put a fence around the pool last spring.
Twelve chairs were set around the long table.
His papers were scattered around the office.
Is there a hardware store around here?
The entrance is around the back of the building.
Her place is just around the corner from mine.
It cost around three hundred dollars.
Let's say around seven, give or take.
The whole meeting was structured around risk.
There are real questions around the timeline.

entries.ipa: /əˈstraɪd/ — the first syllable is always /ə/ and never stressed
entries.register: formal or literary; common in journalism and military writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (she rode astride).
entries.pattern: [sit / ride / stand] astride [noun phrase] · [place or thing] astride [line or route]
entries.contrast: Astride demands two sides straddled, which across does not require: a bridge is across a river because it spans it, but a city is astride a border because it has territory on both sides. Over is the weaker word: it may cover a thing and even touch it (a blanket over the rail), but it never claims a leg or a side on each side of it, which is the entire content of astride (sitting astride the rail). Note the adverbial use, which in equestrian contexts means riding astride rather than sidesaddle.
entries.meaning: With one leg, one side, or one part on each side of something. The literal sense is equestrian, and the figurative sense keeps the geometry exactly: a town astride a highway has buildings on both sides of it. Strategic and geopolitical writing likes the word because it implies control of what passes between. Senses: 1. With a leg on each side of something. 2. Extending on both sides of a line, route, or boundary.
examples: He rode astride a borrowed mare all afternoon.
The child sat astride his father's shoulders.
The village lies astride the old post road.
The refinery sprawls astride the county line.
A single garrison stood astride the only pass.

entries.ipa: /daʊn/ — no reduced form; down destresses without changing its vowel
entries.register: neutral; the "farther along" sense is characteristically American and informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Down is also an adverb, a verb particle, an adjective, a noun, and a verb — the preposition is the only one with an object, and you cannot move it: ran down the hill has no ran the hill down.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] down [linear object] · [verb] down [linear object] · down the street / road / hall · down south / down the coast
entries.contrast: In American English down the street usually has nothing to do with elevation — it means farther along, away from here. Against below and under, which are pure vertical position with no path involved. The British attributable-to sense (that's down to the weather) is not American; Americans say because of, due to, or up to you.
entries.meaning: At or toward a lower point on something, or simply farther along it. American usage has largely bleached the elevation out of the second sense — you go down to the corner store on flat ground — which leaves down functioning as a vague marker of distance from the speaker, paired with up in a way that is regional as much as geographic. Once distance along a line is all the word carries, it takes the last short step and starts measuring distance in time: down the road is next year. Senses: 1. At a lower point on a slope or a vertical surface. 2. Farther along; away from here (no elevation implied). 3. Toward the south, or along a coast or river (regional and idiomatic). 4. Lower in a list, a ranking, or a sequence. 5. Later in time, in the fixed down the road and down the line.
examples: The trailhead is a quarter mile down the ridge.
Water was running down the outside of the foundation.
The pharmacy is two blocks down the street.
His office is down the hall on the left.
Her family is down south for the winter.
We drove down the coast as far as Big Sur.
He is third down the depth chart and unlikely to play.
The Dodgers slid two spots down the standings in a week.
That shortcut will cost somebody money down the road.
Two owners down the line, nobody remembered the handshake deal.

entries.ipa: /ɔf/, also /ɑf/ — no reduced form; the vowel stays full
entries.register: neutral; off of is standard American speech and is deleted in edited prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (the lid came off), an adjective (the milk is off, his timing is off), a noun, a verb, and a very productive particle (call it off, put it off) — none of which takes an object, and the preposition always does: he is off is the adjective, he is off his game is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] off [noun phrase] · [noun] off [noun phrase] · off the coast of [place] · off [substance] · off [standard]
entries.contrast: Two usage points. Off of: get off the couch is the written form and get off of the couch is what people say; the of is redundant and editors remove it. Off from is simply wrong. Against from, which names a source without implying prior contact — she took it from the shelf versus she took it off the shelf.
variants: off of — ubiquitous in American speech, absent from edited prose; off from is nonstandard everywhere
entries.meaning: No longer on, or at a remove from, something it was attached to or aligned with. The static senses gathered here all describe the state after separation: a lid not on its jar, a room opening off a corridor, an island at a distance from a coast, a person no longer using a substance, a performance no longer at its usual level. Senses: 1. Not on; separated from a surface it was resting on. 2. Opening from or branching out of. 3. At a distance from, especially seaward of a coast. 4. No longer using or consuming. 5. Below the usual standard.
examples: Keep the dog off the furniture.
One shutter had come off the front window.
The pantry opens off the back hallway.
Their driveway runs off County Road 12.
The wreck lies four miles off Cape Hatteras.
They anchored just off the point.
She's been off dairy since January.
He went off his medication without telling anyone.
The pitcher was off his game from the first inning.
Sales for the quarter came in off last year's pace.

entries.ipa: /aʊt/ — no reduced form
entries.complement: A restricted noun phrase. As a bare preposition in American English, out takes essentially only openings (out the window, out the door) and a few direction and route nouns (out Route 9, out back, out west). For everything else American English requires out of. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (the fire went out), an adjective (the truth is out), a noun (a called third strike is an out), a verb (the story outed him), and a very productive particle (hand it out, figure it out) — none of which takes an object, and the preposition always does: he leaned out is the adverb, he leaned out the window is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [verb] out [opening] · [live / drive] out [route or direction] · out back / out west / out east
entries.contrast: This is one of the sharpest American/British splits in the class. Americans say he leaned out the window; the British say out of the window. In American English the bare form is preferred with openings. With containers, sources, and materials you need out of on both sides of the Atlantic.
variants: out of — the general-purpose form; see out of
entries.meaning: Through an opening to the outside, or along a route leading away from a center. Bare prepositional out is a narrow word with a strong American accent: it lives on windows, doors, and highways, and it hands everything else to out of. Its enormous life as an adverb, adjective, noun, and particle is separate and is not the preposition. Senses: 1. Through an opening to the outside. 2. Along a road or in a direction leading away from town.
examples: Don't throw anything out the car window.
He walked out the side door without a word.
Smoke was pouring out the vent.
Their place is a few miles out the old highway.
The dogs are out back if you want to see them.
Her people are all out west somewhere.

entries.ipa: /raʊnd/; the apostrophe spelling 'round marks it as a clipping of around
entries.register: chiefly British as a general preposition; in American English it survives only in fixed phrases
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — the same range as around. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb, adjective, noun, and verb, all fully standard in American English; only the general prepositional use is British.
entries.pattern: round [noun phrase] (British) · American fixed forms only: round the clock, year-round, round-trip, round about · British, not American: round the bend, all round
entries.contrast: Americans write around. Round the corner, round the table, and round the block are British. What American English keeps is a short list of frozen forms: round the clock, year-round, round-trip, and the dated approximating round about. Do not take round the bend (crazy) or all-round for American forms — both are British, and the American equivalents are around the bend and all-around.
variants: around — the American form; use it everywhere except in the fixed phrases listed here
entries.meaning: A reduced form of around that became a separate word. In British English it is the ordinary preposition for encircling and vicinity; in American English it has been almost entirely displaced by around and remains only where it is locked into a compound or an idiom. Learners should recognize it and write around. Senses: 1. British: around, in every physical sense. 2. American: in fixed phrases and compounds only.
examples: British usage: they sat round the kitchen table. American: around the kitchen table.
British usage: the shop is just round the corner. American: around the corner.
British usage: by the third week he was going round the bend. American: around the bend.
Dispatchers staffed the line round the clock for six days.
The resort is open year-round.
We booked a round-trip out of Denver and drove from there.

entries.ipa: /θruˈaʊt/, weak /θrəˈaʊt/ — the initial cluster is /θr/, not /tr/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb with no object (the house has hardwood throughout).
entries.pattern: throughout [bounded space] · throughout [organization or region] · [noun phrase] ... throughout (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: Against through: through traces a path in one side and out the other, throughout saturates every part with no path at all. Water ran through the house is a leak; water damage throughout the house is an insurance claim. All over is the spoken equivalent.
entries.meaning: In every part of a space or a body. The word is built to be exhaustive — it claims completeness in a way in and across do not — which is why it belongs to inspection reports, specifications, and any prose that needs to say everywhere inside this thing, with no exceptions. Senses: 1. In every part of a space or a structure. 2. In every part of an organization, a region, or a body.
examples: The original tile is intact throughout the first floor.
Smoke detectors are required throughout the residence.
Recycling bins are placed throughout the campus.
Morale improved throughout the company after the announcement.
The species is found throughout the Southwest.

entries.ipa: /ʌp/ — no weak form; the lax /ʌ/ has nothing further to reduce to, so unstressed up just loses its beat
entries.register: neutral; the "farther along" sense is characteristically American and informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Up is also an adverb, a verb particle, an adjective, a noun, and a verb. The particle/preposition test is movement: you can say ran a bill up but not ran the hill up, because in ran up the hill the hill is the object of the preposition.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] up [linear object] · [verb] up [linear object] · up the street / road / coast · up north
entries.contrast: The mirror of down, and it inherits the same American quirk: up the block usually implies no elevation at all, only distance in a direction the speaker treats as away. Against above and atop, which are static height with no path. Up is far more often a particle than a preposition, and the movement test settles it.
entries.meaning: At or toward a higher point on something, or simply farther along it in the direction the speaker treats as away. As with down, American usage has drained most of the elevation out of the everyday sense, leaving a vague directional marker that pairs with down and varies by region — New Yorkers go up to the Bronx, New Englanders up to Maine, and neither is about altitude. What is left of the vertical idea survives cleanly in rankings and in two idioms that keep an object and therefore keep the preposition: up your alley, up the creek. Senses: 1. At a higher point on a slope or a vertical surface. 2. Farther along; away from here (no elevation implied). 3. Toward the north, or inland along a river or coast. 4. Higher in a ranking, a scale, or a sequence. 5. In the fixed idioms up someone's alley and up the creek.
examples: Their mailbox is halfway up the driveway.
There's a crack running up the chimney.
The laundromat is two doors up the street.
She works at a shop up the road from here.
We drove up the coast to Mendocino.
His family summers up north on the lake.
He worked his way up the ladder from the loading dock.
The song climbed up the chart for six straight weeks.
A restoration that size is right up his alley.
If the loan falls through we are up the creek.
